newsitem.title: USA: US Thrift regulator asks for Internet guidance.
newsitem.headline: US Thrift regulator asks for Internet guidance.

text.p: The regulator of U.S. savings and loan institutions said on Monday that it needed outside advice to help craft policies for the evolving world of electronic banking on the Internet.

Office of Thrift Supervision, facing a growing barrage of questions from savings and loans about the applicability of existing regulations in cyberspace, will publish a request for comments April 2, director Nicholas Retsinas said.
Instead of issuing proposed rules, the agency will issue a less developed "Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking" that asks questions without suggesting answers.
"Washington doesn't always know better," Retsinas said at a press briefing here. "This is an evolving issue. This is an issue that we need to listen and make sure we are as inclusive as possible."

The release will cover home banking on personal computers, automated loan machines, stored-value cards also known as smart cards, and the use of computer "artificial intelligence" software in lending decisions.
Thrifts have asked the agency whether they may provide banking services over the Internet, issue loans from machines in remote locations, or open accounts for overseas depositors.
Thrifts have also asked how they should apply the Community Reinvestment Act, a 1977 law requiring banks to make loans in the communities where they take deposits, to Internet accounts.

The Office of Thrift Supervision was the first U.S. regulator to approve a virtual bank, an institution that has no branches but offers its services over the Internet. In May 1995, the agency approved an application from Security First Network Bank to move to cyberspace.
Commenters will have 60 days to submit responses. The agency plans to study the comments and possibly issue proposed rules for electronic banking, Retsinas said.
